abandon: The mechanism needs the RL model to write line-start 'Answer:' markers before it verifies. Wang's rule reads a line-start 'Answer:' first and falls back to the LAST box. A model that only boxes is therefore read at its final marker, and earlier provisional boxes cannot cost it anything. The board shows the RL model does not write 'Answer:' lines; the base does. knowledge-499152: "'Answer:' line share base 0.44, RL 0.00" and "the base ends with an 'Answer:' line in 39-46 % of answers and RL boxes". knowledge-8229be: every arm that recovers RL accuracy takes RL's format, "'Answer:' line in 0-4 % of answers vs 39-46 % for base-like arms" (knowledge-69adda says the same). result-fdc8da: at the answer start RL gives the 'Answer:' form a log-prob gap of "'Answer:' line median -8.36 (n=132, 121 right)", against \boxed "0.000 (n=338)", so RL actively avoids that marker. result-c57b51: a gold-equal value sits in the last 5 lines of "31 of 2,000 base samples", "against 5 for RL", so RL rarely loses a right value while stating its answer. A first-marker rule can only hit the model that writes 'Answer:' lines, and that model is the base. result-60d899 already shows the literal rule costing the base: "a literal reading of their rule ... 336-355" against v3 405-418. So the direction the mechanism needs (the rule costs RL more than the base) is reversed on the measured pair. The one escape is that Wang's 3.0 release formats answers differently from 3.1. No item supports that. knowledge-8a31ad (7) says 3.1 differs from 3.0 only "by completion length 16k instead of 12k and by not masking truncated sequences", with the same reward and prompt. result-9d979a finds Math 3.0 and 3.1 are each other's nearest neighbours in weight subspace ("Math 3.0 with Math 3.1 0.476"). Using this mechanism to explain the Wang parity would require a 3.0 'Answer:' habit that nothing on the board shows and every format measurement argues against.
